transcript.text: Today we’re pleased to have on the show Alice Bussell from the Dolphin Conservation Trust.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Tell us about the Trust, Alice.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Well, obviously its purpose is to protect dolphins in seas all around the world.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: It tries to raise people’s awareness of the problems these marine creatures are suffering because of pollution and other threats.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: It started ten years ago and it’s one of the fastest growing animal charities in the country – although it’s still fairly small compared with the big players in animal protection.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: We are particularly proud of the work we do in education – last year we visited a huge number of schools in different parts of the country, going round to talk to children and young people aged from five to eighteen.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: In fact, about thirty-five per cent of our members are children.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: The charity uses its money to support campaigns – for example, for changes in fishing policy and so forth.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: It hopes soon to be able to employ its first full-time biologist – with dolphin expertise – to monitor populations.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Of course, many people give their services on a voluntary basis and we now have volunteers working in observation, office work and other things.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I should also tell you about the award we won from the Charity Commission last year – for our work in education.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Although it’s not meant an enormous amount of money for us, it has made our activities even more widely publicised and understood.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: In the long term it may not bring in extra members but we’re hoping it’ll have this effect.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Is it possible to see dolphins in UK waters?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: In several locations.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: And we have a big project in the east part of Scotland.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: This has long been a haven for dolphins because it has very little shipping.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: However, that may be about to change soon because oil companies want to increase exploration there.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: We’re campaigning against this because, although there’ll be little pollution from oil, exploration creates a lot of underwater noise.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: It means the dolphins can’t rest and socialise.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: This is how I became interested in dolphin conservation in the first place.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I had never seen one and I hadn’t been particularly interested in them at school.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Then I came across this story about a family of dolphins who had to leave their home in the Moray Firth because of the oil companies and about a child who campaigned to save them.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I couldn’t put the book down – I was hooked.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I’m sure our listeners will want to find out what they can do to help.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: You mentioned the ‘Adopt a Dolphin’ scheme.
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Can you tell us about that?
transcript.speaker: INTERVIEWER

transcript.text: Of course!
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: People can choose one of our dolphins to sponsor.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: They receive a picture of it and news updates.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I’d like to tell you about four which are currently being adopted by our members: Moondancer, Echo, Kiwi and Samson.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Unfortunately, Echo is being rather elusive this year and hasn’t yet been sighted by our observers but we remain optimistic that he’ll be out there soon.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: All the others have been out in force – Samson and Moondancer are often photographed together but it is Kiwi who’s our real ‘character’ as she seems to love coming up close for the cameras and we’ve captured her on film hundreds of times.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: They all have their own personalities – Moondancer is very elegant and curves out and into the water very smoothly, whereas Samson has a lot of energy – he’s always leaping out of the water with great vigour.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: You’d probably expect him to be the youngest – he’s not quite – that’s Kiwi – but Samson’s the latest of our dolphins to be chosen for the scheme.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Kiwi makes a lot of noise so we can often pick her out straightaway.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Echo and Moondancer are noisy too, but Moondancer’s easy to find because she has a particularly large fin on her back, which makes her easy to identify.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: So, yes, they’re all very different …
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Well, they sound a fascinating group …

transcript.text: Today, I want to talk about self-regulatory focus theory and how the actions of leaders can affect the way followers approach different situations.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Self-regulatory focus theory is a theory developed by Tori Higgins.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He says that a person’ focus at any given time is to either approach pleasure or avoid pain.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These are two basic motivations that each and every one of us has, and they cause us to have different kinds of goals.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Promotion goals in different life situations emphasise achievement.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Prevention goals are oriented towards the avoidance of punishment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In a specific situation, our thoughts might focus more on promotion goals or more on prevention goals.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The theory suggests that two factors affect which goals we are focusing on.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: First, there is a chronic factor.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This factor is connected to a person’s personality and says that each person has a basic tendency to either focus more on promotion goals or focus more on prevention goals as part of his or her personality.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Second, there is a situational factor which means that the context we are in can make us more likely to focus on one set of goals or the other.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, we are more likely to be thinking about pleasure and to have promotion goals when we are spending time with a friend.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In contrast, if we are working on an important project for our boss, we are more likely to try to avoid making mistakes and therefore have more prevention goals in our mind.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Research has shown that the goals we are focusing on at a given time affect the way we think.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, when focusing on promotion goals, people consider their ideal self, their aspirations and gains.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They don’t think about what they can lose, so they think in a happier mode.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They feel more inspired to change.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: When people are focusing on prevention goals, they think about their “ought” self.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: What are they supposed to be?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: What are people expecting from them?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They consider their obligations to others.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As a result, they experience more anxiety and try to avoid situations where they could lose.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now that I have talked about the two focuses and how they affect people, I want to look at the idea that the way leaders behave, or their style of leading, can affect the focus that followers adopt in a specific situation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In talking about leadership, we often mention transformational leaders and transactional leaders.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Transformational leaders, when interacting with their followers, focus on their development.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In their words and actions transformational leaders highlight change.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Their speech is passionate and conveys a definitive vision.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: All of these things can encourage followers to think about what could be.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In other words, they inspire a promotion focus in their followers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In contrast, transactional leaders focus on developing clear structures that tell their followers exactly what is expected of them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: While they do explain the rewards people will get for following orders, they emphasise more how a follower will be punished or that a follower won’t get rewarded if his or her behaviour doesn’t change.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In short, they emphasise the consequences of making a mistake.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This emphasis will clearly lead followers to focus on avoiding punishment and problems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is clearly a prevention focus.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In conclusion, it is important to understand that one focus is not necessarily better than the other one.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For a designer who works in a field where a lot of innovation is needed, a promotion focus is probably better.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In contrast, a prevention focus which causes people to work more cautiously and produce higher quality work might be very appropriate for a job like a surgeon, for example.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The main point of the research, though, is that the actions of leaders can greatly influence whether people approach a situation with more of a promotion focus or more of a prevention focus.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
